panels.title: SLO status — is this service in trouble right now
Availability SLI (5m)
panels.description: Share of requests in the last 5 minutes that did not return 5xx. Red below the 99.5% objective. 4xx is excluded on purpose — a client asking for a product that does not exist is not this service failing.

panels.title: Latency SLI (5m)
panels.description: Share of requests served in under 400 ms, counted from the le="0.4" histogram bucket rather than estimated with histogram_quantile. 0.4 is an exact bucket boundary, so this is a count and not an interpolation. Red below the 99% objective.

panels.title: Availability budget left (30d)
panels.description: How much of the 30-day error budget is unspent. Goes negative once the SLO has been missed for the period — at which point the question is not whether to page but whether to stop shipping.

panels.title: Latency budget left (30d)
panels.description: Same accounting as the availability budget, against the 99%-under-400 ms objective. On a cluster younger than 30 days this is computed over whatever data exists, so treat it as directional early on.

panels.title: Availability burn rate
panels.description: Multiples of the sustainable burn, over 5m. Under 1 the budget is recovering; at 14.4 the whole 30-day budget would be gone in ~50 hours, which is the page threshold.

panels.title: Latency burn rate
panels.description: Latency budgets are 20x larger than storefront's availability budget (5% vs 0.5%), so a latency burn rate of 14.4 means a much larger absolute share of requests is slow than the same number would mean for errors. Compare the multiple, not the underlying ratio.

panels.title: Request rate by route
panels.description: Traffic shape first: a burn rate that spiked while this collapsed is a denominator artefact, not a reliability problem. `route` is the route template, so /products/17 and /products/18 share one series. Probe and scrape traffic is never recorded, so nothing here is guaranteed-success filler.

panels.title: Error rate
panels.description: 5xx as a percentage of requests. The dashed line is the 0.5% error budget — sustained time above it burns budget faster than 30 days allows. The per-route series is the useful one: a single route above the line points at a handler, all routes above it points at the pod, the node, or an injected fault.

panels.title: Latency percentiles
panels.description:
Percentiles, NOT the SLI. histogram_quantile interpolates inside a bucket, so these numbers are estimates and the p99 in particular is only as precise as the bucket it lands in. Read this panel for shape — which percentile moved, and by how much — and read the SLI compliance panel next to it for the number the SLO is actually judged on.

The dashed line is the 400 ms SLO threshold. p99 crossing it is roughly the moment the latency SLI starts failing, since the objective is 99% under that threshold.

panels.title: SLI compliance — % of requests under 400 ms
panels.description:
The bucket ratio the latency SLO is defined on: a count of requests that landed in the le="0.4" bucket over all requests. Exact, because 0.4 is a bucket boundary in svc_common.metrics.LATENCY_BUCKETS. This is the same arithmetic Sloth records, computed here at the panel's own resolution.

Dashed line at the 99% objective. Time under the line is time spending latency budget.

panels.title: Requests by status code
panels.description: Separates the two failure stories the error-rate panel blends. A wall of 500 is the service or an injected fault; a wall of 503 from storefront is an upstream it could not reach; a rise in 4xx is the caller, and is deliberately outside the SLI.

panels.title: Burn rate — why the alert fired
Availability burn rate — alert windows
panels.description:
Availability SLO, error budget 0.50%.

Each series is the error ratio over one alert window divided by the SLO's error budget, i.e. Sloth's own burn-rate arithmetic — so the y axis is a multiple and the dashed lines are literally the alert thresholds.

1x = burning budget exactly as fast as 30 days allows. 6x and 14.4x are the two page conditions from the SRE workbook table.

A page fires when BOTH halves of a pair are above their line at the same time: 5m AND 1h above 14.4x, or 30m AND 6h above 6x. The short window is what stops an already-recovered incident from firing off the long window's tail — so if the 5m series has dropped back under the line while 1h is still above it, the alert is about to resolve and the incident is over.

panels.title: Latency burn rate — alert windows
panels.description:
Latency SLO, error budget 5.00%.

Each series is the error ratio over one alert window divided by the SLO's error budget, i.e. Sloth's own burn-rate arithmetic — so the y axis is a multiple and the dashed lines are literally the alert thresholds.

1x = burning budget exactly as fast as 30 days allows. 6x and 14.4x are the two page conditions from the SRE workbook table.

A page fires when BOTH halves of a pair are above their line at the same time: 5m AND 1h above 14.4x, or 30m AND 6h above 6x. The short window is what stops an already-recovered incident from firing off the long window's tail — so if the 5m series has dropped back under the line while 1h is still above it, the alert is about to resolve and the incident is over.

panels.title: Dependencies — is this our fault or theirs
Dependency call rate by outcome
panels.description:
The panel that answers "is storefront broken, or is something downstream broken" without opening a trace. `outcome` is ok, timeout, transport_error, or http_4xx/http_5xx.

A rise in `recs · timeout` alongside a flat catalog leg and a storefront latency burn is the slow-dependency scenario: recs is late, storefront waits, the fan-out costs the slower leg. A rise in `catalog · http_5xx` with storefront 503s is the hard-failure scenario — storefront degrades around recs but cannot degrade around a missing product.

panels.title: Dependency latency percentiles
panels.description:
Outbound call duration as seen by storefront, so it includes network and queueing the dependency's own dashboard will not show. Estimates (histogram_quantile), not an SLI.

The dashed line at 2s is DEFAULT_TIMEOUT's read timeout in svc_common.http — a dependency p99 pressed against it is producing `timeout` outcomes rather than slow successes, and the client is giving up before the dependency answers.

panels.title: Pods — is it the code or the container
In-flight requests
panels.description: Concurrency per pod. Climbing while request rate is flat means requests are taking longer and workers are piling up — the shape that turns a slow dependency into an outage. One pod far above the others is a load-balance or a stuck-worker problem rather than a service-wide one.

panels.title: Container restarts
panels.description: Cumulative, so every step up is one restart. Restarts concurrent with a burn usually mean OOMKill (check the memory panel — memory is limited, CPU deliberately is not) or a failing liveness probe. Note that liveness is intentionally slow to act (~60s of failures) so a dependency outage does not get masked by Kubernetes healing the pod: restarts during a dependency incident are a real anomaly, not the expected behaviour.

panels.title: Container memory (working set)
panels.description: Working set against the container's memory limit. The limit is the line that matters: memory is the one resource that is capped, so approaching it means OOMKill and a restart, which shows up in the panel to the left and as 5xx in the SLI.

panels.title: Container CPU
panels.description: Cores. There is deliberately no CPU limit on these containers, so there is no throttling line to cross and this is a saturation signal rather than a cause of latency. If CPU is flat while latency climbs, the time is being spent waiting — on a dependency, or on the injected sleep.

panels.title: Warnings and errors
panels.description:
Warnings and errors only — the lines worth reading while a burn-rate alert is open. Each line carries trace_id; click it and the Loki datasource's derived field opens the trace in Tempo.

LABEL NAMES ARE THE UNCERTAIN PART OF THIS PANEL. Logs reach Loki as OTLP through the collector, so the stream labels are Loki's OTLP resource-attribute mapping (dots become underscores), not Kubernetes label names. `service_name` is used here because the Tempo datasource in the kube-prometheus-stack values maps service.name -> service_name for its trace-to-logs link, so that is the name this cluster already assumes.

If the panel is empty, work down this list:
1. Swap the selector for the hidden query B below ({k8s_namespace_name="demo", k8s_container_name="..."}) — those come from the k8sattributes processor.
2. Drop `| json`. If the OTLP body arrived structured rather than as a raw JSON string, `level` is already a field (or is `severity_text` / `detected_level`) and the json parser produces nothing to filter on.
3. Confirm anything is arriving at all with a bare `{service_name=~".+"}` in Explore, then read the real label names off a result.

Wider caveat: svc_common.logging writes JSON to stdout and the collector's logs pipeline has only an OTLP receiver (no filelog receiver / logsCollection preset), so if nothing in the app exports logs over OTLP this panel is empty because no logs are reaching Loki at all, not because the labels are wrong.

panels.title: Injected faults
panels.description:
The cause, on the same time axis as its effect. `error` is a request turned into a 500 before the handler ran; `latency` is a request delayed by FAULT_LATENCY_MS. Both are counted by the metrics middleware, so an injected fault is guaranteed to appear in the SLI above — a fault the SLI cannot see would not be worth injecting.

Empty is the normal state: fault_injected_total is created lazily on first injection, so before any chaos run the series does not exist and the panel reads No data. During an experiment, the shoulder here should line up with the shoulder on the burn-rate panels.

title: storefront · service SLO
description:
storefront is the only service behind the Ingress, so a burn here is the one a customer would feel. GET /products/{product_id} fans out to catalog and recs concurrently, so it costs the slower leg, not the sum — the dependency row is where that shows up.

Read top to bottom: the stat row says whether to care, the RED row says what changed, the burn-rate row says why the alert fired, and the dependency and pod rows say whose fault it is.
